title: HTTPS and the Padlock
about: How your connection to a website is kept secret, and what the padlock means.

cards.prompt:
On café Wi-Fi you log in to a **plain [[HTTP]]** site (no S). Your [[packets|packet]] pass the café's [[router]], then many more run by strangers.

Who could read your password?

options.text: Anyone running a device on the route, like the café
Only the website, since it's addressed there
options.nudge: An address doesn't stop others reading, any more than on a postcard: who handles it on the way?

options.text: Nobody, because the password box hides it
options.nudge: The dots only hide it on your screen; plain HTTP travels as readable text.

options.text: Only the café, since you joined its Wi-Fi
options.nudge: The café's router is only the first stop: many more come after it.

cards.explanation: Plain HTTP is a **postcard**: your password travels as readable text through **every** device on the route. The dots only hide it on your screen, not on the [[network]].
cards.hint: Plain HTTP is a postcard: who handles a postcard on its way?

cards.title: HTTPS: HTTP in a locked box
cards.body:
**HTTPS** is [[HTTP]] carried inside another [[protocol]], **TLS**, which **encrypts** it: scrambles it with secret keys only your [[browser]] and the [[server]] have. To routers in between, it's random noise.

HTTPS uses [[port]] **443** (plain HTTP uses 80), and browsers show a **padlock** beside the address.

cards.prompt:
TLS does its own [[handshake]]: keys are agreed, and the server shows its **certificate**, a digital ID proving it owns the name, issued by a **certificate authority** your [[browser]] trusts.

Put the steps of loading an HTTPS page in order.

items.label: Browser sends an encrypted GET request

cards.explanation: TCP opens the connection first, then the **TLS handshake** agrees keys and checks the certificate. Only then does any HTTP travel, all of it encrypted.
cards.hint: A connection must be open before it's secured, and secure before anything private travels.
cards.nudge: TLS needs TCP's connection open first, and the request needs the keys agreed.

cards.prompt: Match each thing you want to the part of [[HTTPS]] that does it.

pairs.left: Stop the café reading your password
Prove the server really is example.com
Vouch that a certificate is genuine
Check at a glance that you're encrypted

cards.explanation: **Encryption** keeps what you send private, the **certificate** is the server's ID, a **certificate authority** vouches for it, and the **padlock** shows the connection is encrypted.
cards.hint: Scrambling, an ID card, whoever issues ID cards, and an icon in the address bar.
cards.nudge: Don't mix up the ID card with who issues it: the server shows one, the authority vouches for it.

cards.prompt:
A padlock means the connection is encrypted and the server owns the **name in the address**, nothing about who runs it.

Tap the **one** thing here that the padlock vouches for.
cards.explanation: The certificate only backs the **address**: this server belongs to whoever owns `login-check.example`. The logo and banner are just drawn on the page, so this padlocked site isn't Your Bank at all.
cards.hint: A certificate is an ID card for a name: which part shows the site's real name?
cards.nudge: The logo and banner are page parts anyone could draw: the certificate is about something your browser shows.

cards.prompt: A login page at `examp1e.com` (with a digit 1) shows a **padlock**. What does it prove?

options.text: It's encrypted to examp1e.com's owner, nothing more
It's really example.com, checked by an authority
options.nudge: Look at the name: it has a digit 1, and its owner can get a certificate for it.

options.text: Your password is safe, since nobody can read it
options.nudge: Nobody in between can read it, but whoever runs the site still gets it.

options.text: Your browser checked the site and found no scams
options.nudge: The padlock isn't a scam check: it's about the connection and the name.

cards.explanation: The padlock proves your connection is encrypted to a server that owns the exact name **examp1e.com**, a lookalike. Nobody can read your typing on the way, but the scammer gets it at the other end.
cards.hint: Read the name closely, then remember the two things a padlock means.

cards.prompt:
HTTPS encrypts the whole request, path included. But every [[packet]] shows the server's [[IP address]], and the name usually shows in your [[DNS]] lookup.

On café Wi-Fi you change your password at `https://example.com/account/settings`. What can the café see?

options.text: Which site you're on, but not the page or what you type

options.nudge: The address starts with `https`, so what you send is encrypted. The café can't read your new password.

options.text: The page /account/settings, but not the new password
options.nudge: The path is part of the HTTP request, and with HTTPS the whole request is encrypted.

options.text: Nothing at all, not even which site you're on
options.nudge: Packets still need an address on the outside to be delivered. What does that address give away?

cards.explanation: The **path** and your typing are inside the [[encrypted|encryption]] request. But the address is on every packet and the name usually shows too, so the café can tell **which site**, not which page or what you send.
cards.hint: Split it into what's inside the encrypted request and what has to stay on the outside of each packet.

cards.prompt:
A certificate must be in date, issued for the name you visited, and from an authority your [[browser]] trusts.

Match each warning to what went wrong.

pairs.right: Its valid dates have run out
It was issued for a different name
No trusted authority vouches for it

cards.explanation: Each warning means one check failed: the **dates**, the **name** or a **trusted issuer**. On a site where you'd log in or pay, don't click past it.
cards.hint: Three checks, three warnings: dates, names, and who issued it.
cards.nudge: Read each warning's own words: one is about time, one the name, one who issued it.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **HTTPS** is [[HTTP]] inside **TLS**: encrypted between [[browser]] and [[server]].
- A **certificate** proves the server owns the name in the address.
- The padlock means **encrypted**, not **honest**: scam sites have one too.

Next: the grand tour. Everything in this course, in one click.
